text: Adults: The usual starting dose of metformin hydrochloride tablets is 500 mg twice a day or 850 mg once a day, given with meals. Dosage increases should be made in increments of 500 mg weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks, up to a total of 2000 mg per day, given in divided doses. The maximum recommended daily dose is 2550 mg in adults.

Metformin hydrochloride tablets should be taken in divided doses with meals to reduce gastrointestinal side effects. Patients receiving 2000 mg or more per day may respond better to three times a day dosing with meals.

Overdose of metformin hydrochloride has occurred, including ingestion of amounts greater than 50 grams. Hypoglycemia was reported in approximately 10% of cases. Lactic acidosis has been reported in approximately 32% of metformin overdose cases.

WARNING: LACTIC ACIDOSIS. Postmarketing cases of metformin-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. Risk factors include renal impairment, concomitant use of certain drugs, age 65 years old or greater, having a radiological study with contrast, surgery and other procedures, hypoxic states, excessive alcohol intake, and hepatic impairment.
The most common adverse reactions (greater than 5%) are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, asthenia, indigestion, abdominal discomfort, and headache.

Adults and children 12 years and over: take 1 tablet (200 mg) every 4 to 6 hours while symptoms persist. If pain or fever does not respond to 1 tablet, 2 tablets may be used. Do not exceed 6 tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor. The smallest effective dose should be used.

Prescription strength: for mild to moderate pain, 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours as necessary. For rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis, 1200 mg to 3200 mg daily (300 mg four times a day; 400 mg, 600 mg or 800 mg three or four times a day). Doses greater than 3200 mg total daily dose are not recommended.

Symptoms of overdose may include nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, drowsiness, headache, tinnitus, and in severe cases gastrointestinal bleeding, hypotension, and acute kidney injury. In case of overdose, get medical help or contact a Poison Control Center right away.

WARNING: RISK OF SERIOUS CARDIOVASCULAR AND GASTROINTESTINAL EVENTS. NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke. NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal.

The most frequent type of adverse reaction occurring with ibuprofen is gastrointestinal: nausea, epigastric pain, heartburn, diarrhea, abdominal distress, indigestion, constipation, abdominal cramps or pain, fullness of the GI tract. Also reported: dizziness, headache, nervousness, rash, tinnitus, edema, fluid retention.

Individualized dosing: The dosage and administration of warfarin sodium must be individualized for each patient according to the patient's INR response to the drug. Initiate therapy with a dose of 2 mg to 5 mg once daily. Adjust the dose based on INR results. The typical maintenance dose is 2 mg to 10 mg once daily.
Take warfarin sodium at the same time each day. Missed dose: if a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible on the same day. Do not double the dose the next day to make up for a missed dose.

Excessive anticoagulation with or without bleeding is the principal sign of overdose. Bleeding may present as blood in stools or urine, excessive menstrual bleeding, bruising, nosebleeds, or bleeding gums. Contact a healthcare provider immediately.

WARNING: BLEEDING RISK. Warfarin sodium can cause major or fatal bleeding. Perform regular monitoring of INR in all treated patients. Drugs, dietary changes, and other factors affect INR levels achieved with warfarin therapy.

The most serious adverse reactions are hemorrhage and necrosis of skin and other tissues. Other reactions include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, taste perversion, abdominal pain, flatulence, bloating, rash, hair loss, and cold intolerance.

Hypertension: The recommended initial dose is 10 mg once daily. The usual dosage range is 20 mg to 40 mg per day administered in a single daily dose. Doses up to 80 mg have been used but do not appear to give greater effect.
Heart failure: The recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily. Increase as tolerated to a maximum of 40 mg once daily. Lisinopril may be taken with or without food.
The most likely manifestation of overdosage would be hypotension, for which the usual treatment would be intravenous infusion of normal saline solution.

WARNING: FETAL TOXICITY. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue lisinopril as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.
The most common adverse reactions are headache, dizziness, cough, hypotension, chest pain, and elevated blood potassium. A persistent dry cough has been reported.

Adults and children 12 years and over: take 2 caplets (500 mg each) every 6 hours while symptoms last. Do not take more than 6 caplets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor. Do not use for more than 10 days unless directed by a doctor.

Liver warning: This product contains acetaminophen. Severe liver damage may occur if you take more than 4,000 mg of acetaminophen in 24 hours, with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using this product. In case of overdose, get medical help or contact a Poison Control Center right away even if you do not notice any signs or symptoms.
Acetaminophen is generally well tolerated at recommended doses. Rare reactions include skin rash, allergic reactions, and, with overdose, liver injury.

Adults and children 12 years and over: take 1 or 2 tablets (325 mg each) with a full glass of water every 4 hours while symptoms persist. Do not take more than 12 tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor.

Stomach bleeding warning: This product contains an NSAID, which may cause severe stomach bleeding. Common reactions include heartburn, nausea, and stomach pain. Ringing in the ears may signal too much aspirin.
